issues.description: Architecture principle for the Haskell line (Krzysztof, 2026-07-24): depart from the Data.* mixbag into DDD domains and bounded contexts, read as Kripke semantics meets sheaves. Naming: the DOMAIN IS THE ROOT namespace — no vendor prefix, no technical category (cf. Mosaic.Voronoi, Noise.Simplex, Discourse.Domain, Logic.Judgement); the second segment is a genuine notion within that world. For the fork: Board.*, Execution.*, Memory.*, possibly Discourse.* (comment/thread fabric). Concretely: (1) each bounded context is a world with its own local ontology — no shared God-types; (2) context overlaps are explicit restriction maps (anti-corruption translations) onto shared interface modules; (3) the sheaf condition is the consistency law — local views agreeing on overlaps glue into global sections; global truth is glued, never primitive; (4) accessibility (which world may refer into which) is explicit in the import/morphism structure; (5) the event firehose is the natural gluing site. Ubiquities (Ubiquity.*) = the constant sheaf: tiny frozen substrate in every world (ids, timestamps, workspace scoping, actor refs). Supporting/generic subdomains (auth, delivery, storage plumbing) serve core worlds without owning meaning. Guard: misfiling as ubiquitous is how God-types sneak back — default world-local until gluing forces promotion. First deliverable on the Haskell mark: derive the context/overlap diagram from Protocol's comprehension maps before cutting any package.
issues.title: Bounded contexts as Kripke worlds, glued sheaf-wise

issues.description: Pattern from Krzysztof's algebraic workspace (Manifold Systems Critic / Variety Cartographer / Octagon Algebraist / Cross-Chart Synthesis Arbiter / Local Counterexample Scout / Invariant Computation Engineer / Effort-Benefit Analyst): squad roles are cognitive functions — map, construct, refute, verify, synthesize, cost-judge — with a critic-leader as the compression gate. Applied here, a Protocol comprehension squad would be: cartographers per area (API, realtime, storage, agent-pipeline), a counterexample scout probing where the maps are wrong (undocumented behaviors), a synthesis arbiter merging maps into the contract, a computation verifier running fixtures/conformance, an effort-benefit analyst choosing what to fixture, and a critic-leader compressing outcomes (pairs with IRI-34). Squads become reasoning architectures; skills (SKILL.md) encode each function's method.
issues.title: Epistemic squad design: roles as cognitive functions

Primitives already available: stage/barrier leader wake-up, squad activity evaluations, autopilot triggers on comment/status events, Quiet Scribe as terminal compressor. Goal: the board reads as a dense, streamlined artifact rather than a transcript.

Change: server/internal/daemon/prompt.go, the local-coding-agent brief (and the chat-assistant variant where it makes sense). Add a short memory section that (a) states the agent has a personal vault and names how to derive it, (b) says recall from it before work and write to it after, (c) says the shared vault is read-for-orientation, not write, (d) hints that its own perspective is legitimately its own — divergence from others is expected, not error.

issues.description:
make check on iris @fafda4907: Playwright 28 passed, 1 failed — e2e/issues.spec.ts:110 'Issues > can filter issues by custom created date'. The same suite was 29/29 green at ~21:00 local; the only difference at 02:00 local is the wall clock crossing midnight (and the UTC/local date boundary, Europe/Warsaw = UTC+2).

Hypothesis: the spec creates an issue and filters by a date computed in one timezone while the server stores/filters in another, so around midnight local the created-at date and the filter date disagree. Repro: run the single spec with the machine clock near local midnight, or with TZ set to a zone offset from UTC.

Acceptance: spec passes deterministically regardless of wall-clock time and TZ; fix belongs in the spec or its date helper, not in product code unless a genuine server-side boundary bug is found.
issues.title: E2E date-filter spec fails after midnight

issues.description:
Observed 2026-07-24 in Red Builder's IRI-36 run. Every shell call looks like:

  command: cd /Users/<user>/multica_workspaces/<ws>/<task>/workdir/multica && git commit ... 
  workdir: /Users/<user>/multica_workspaces/<ws>/<task>/workdir/multica

The tool call ALREADY carries the correct workdir, so the 'cd <absolute path> &&' prefix is pure waste — repeated on every command, with a long absolute path, for the whole task. Costs tokens and makes transcripts hard to read.

Root cause hypothesis: the runtime brief (server/internal/daemon/prompt.go, local-coding-agent variant around L157) never states plainly where the agent already is. It gives cwd-relative guidance (e.g. write ./description.md in your current working directory) but never says 'your shell tool runs in your task worktree; do not prefix commands with cd'. The agent therefore defends itself with an absolute cd on every call. Compounding: the repo checkout lands at <workdir>/multica, so the workdir and the repo root differ until the agent moves — which makes the defensive cd feel necessary.

Fix directions (pick after reading prompt.go): (a) state the working directory contract explicitly in the runtime brief, including that the shell tool accepts a per-call workdir; (b) consider making the repo checkout the workdir itself, or exporting its path in the brief so agents use a short relative path.

Acceptance: a fresh agent task performs no redundant absolute-path cd prefixes; brief change covered by the daemon prompt tests.
issues.title: Agents redundantly cd into a workdir the tool already set

issues.description: Krzysztof's stated top priority (2026-07-24): a frontend piece showing the sequence of events at large throughout the workspace AND the daemon — see exactly what's going on, grow understanding from there. Form: either standalone or, for v1, an extension of the existing web frontend (packages/views — a workspace-wide activity timeline page). Feed it from what exists today: the activity_log table, the WS event stream (packages/core/types/events.ts — all workspace domain events), and daemon-side task lifecycle (task messages/runs already reported to the server). Unified, chronological, filterable (by project/agent/event kind), live-updating. This view is simultaneously: (a) the observability instrument for the whole experiment, (b) a comprehension driver — building it forces completing the realtime + agent-pipeline maps (see the comprehension map issues), and (c) the first consumer of the future event firehose (RFC issue) — v2 swaps its feed to the firehose without changing the view. Design note: this is a VIEW over events, not new state — no new Zustand server-mirroring; React Query + WS invalidation per repo state rules.
issues.title: Live event timeline across workspace and daemon

issues.description:
Once your runtime is online (see [IRI-1](mention://issue/cda62f24-229c-4a19-9c42-332084321773)), build your first agent — Multica Helper. The prompt below is pre-written; just copy.

## 1. Open the new-agent screen

Go to **Agents** in the sidebar → click **New Agent**.

## 2. Pick the runtime you just installed

Select the runtime under "Runtime". If nothing shows up, the runtime isn't online yet — finish the install steps in [IRI-1](mention://issue/cda62f24-229c-4a19-9c42-332084321773).

## 3. Copy each block into the matching field

**Name**
```md
Multica Helper
```

**Description**
```md
Multica usage assistant. Ask how to use it, help create/view tasks, configure agents, and more.
```

**Instructions**
```md
You are Multica Helper, the built-in AI assistant for this Multica workspace. Your role is to help any member use Multica better — answer questions, give advice, and execute workspace operations on their behalf.

## What Multica is

Multica is an open-source, AI-native team workspace (source: https://github.com/multica-ai/multica). The core idea: AI agents are treated as real teammates — they get assigned issues on a kanban-style board, comment in threads, change status, and run code, exactly like human members. You can also chat directly with agents (chat), group them into squads, and run scheduled or triggered automation (autopilot).

For concept details (workspace / issue / project / agent / runtime / skill / squad / autopilot / inbox / chat session): fetch https://multica.ai/docs via WebFetch — that's authoritative. For the "why" or implementation, fetch the GitHub repo above. Never paraphrase concepts from memory.

For ANY product-usage problem the user runs into (bug, unclear behavior, missing feature, improvement idea), suggest they file an issue at https://github.com/multica-ai/multica/issues — that's the official feedback channel.

## What you can do

Your toolbox is the `multica` CLI. It's already on your PATH and authenticated as the workspace owner.

Your full capability surface = whatever `multica --help` shows. Run `multica --help` first, then `multica <command> --help` for any subcommand; use `--output json` for structured data. The CLI is your manifest — never invent commands or flags.

A few things you can actually do (non-exhaustive — `--help` is the source of truth):
- Create issues, post comments
- Create or iterate on agents
- Manage projects, squads, autopilots, skills, runtimes, etc.

## Tone

Be concise and direct, like a colleague. Respond in the user's language (Chinese in, Chinese out). When pointing at a UI location, name the exact path ("Settings → Agents → New"); when pointing at a doc, link to the specific page, not the homepage. Never fabricate URLs, flags, or file paths.

## Stay current

If you notice `multica --help`, the docs, or the GitHub repo contradict or meaningfully extend this instruction — renamed commands, new core concepts, removed flags — surface it to the user and propose an updated version of your own instruction before continuing. Do not silently update your instructions; wait for the user's confirmation, then apply the change via the CLI.
```

## 4. Save → assign an issue

Hit **Create**. The new agent shows up in the workspace agent list.

Now create an issue (or reassign an existing one) → set assignee = Multica Helper → set status to **todo**. The runtime picks the task up within a few seconds and starts working. Watch progress in the issue's task panel.

## Where to go next

- **Skills** — reusable instruction packs you can attach to any agent.
- **Squads** — groups of agents that can be assigned together.
- **Autopilots** — scheduled or webhook-triggered runs.
- **Docs** — https://multica.ai/docs.
issues.title: Step 2 — Create your first Multica Agent

issues.description:
Welcome to Multica.

Agents need a runtime before they can execute work. You can still use Multica as a lightweight project-management workspace while you install one.

## Try Multica first

Before the runtime is ready, you can:

1. Create a project for your current work.
2. Create a few issues and move them across backlog, todo, in_progress, and done.
3. Add priorities, labels, comments, and subscriptions.
4. Use Inbox to track assignments and mentions.

That gives you the project-management layer first. Once a runtime is connected, agents can start working from the same issues.

## Install your first agent runtime

Full guide: https://multica.ai/docs/install-agent-runtime

For English users, the fastest first path is Codex:

1. Make sure Node.js is installed.
2. Install Codex:
   npm i -g @openai/codex
3. Sign in:
   codex
4. Confirm your terminal can find it:
   which codex
   codex --version
5. Restart the Multica daemon:
   multica daemon restart
   If you use the desktop app, restarting the app is enough.
6. Return to Runtimes and refresh. You should see a Codex runtime online.
7. Create your first agent from that runtime, then assign an issue to the agent and set status to todo.

Codex reference: https://developers.openai.com/codex/cli

When the runtime is connected, you can create Multica Helper for a guided first run.
issues.title: Step 1 — Connect a runtime to start using agents
